title: Designing a social network graph

facts.text: A user searches for someone and sees the shortest path to that person; the service must be highly available.
Assumptions: traffic is uneven, some searches are more popular than others, the graph data will not fit on a single machine, and graph edges are unweighted.
The scale is 100 million users with 50 friends each on average, giving 5 billion friend relationships, and 1 billion friend searches per month, or 400 search requests per second.
The exercise avoids graph-specific solutions such as GraphQL or a graph database like Neo4j; without that constraint, a graph database or graph query language could be used.
Without millions of users (vertices) and billions of friend relationships (edges), a general breadth-first search (BFS) would solve this unweighted shortest path task.
Users cannot all fit on one machine, so they are sharded across Person Servers, which are accessed through a Lookup Service.
The client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Search API server, which forwards to the User Graph Service.

The User Graph Service asks the Lookup Service for the Person Server holding the current user, retrieves that user's friend_ids, and runs a BFS with the user as source and the friend_ids as adjacent nodes.
For each adjacent node it must again ask the Lookup Service which Person Server stores that id, a step with potential for optimization.
The public API is REST; internal communication could use remote procedure calls.

Person data can be served from a memory cache such as Redis or Memcached, which cuts response times and downstream traffic at 400 average read requests per second (higher at peak), especially for repeated searches and well-connected people.
Complete or partial BFS traversals can be stored in the memory cache to speed later lookups, or computed offline in batch and stored in a NoSQL database.
Reduce machine jumps by batching friend lookups hosted on the same Person Server, and shard Person Servers by location, since friends generally live closer to each other.
Run two BFS searches at once, one from the source and one from the destination, then merge the two paths.
Start the BFS from people with many friends, since they more likely shorten the degrees of separation to the target, and set a time or hop limit before asking the user whether to keep searching.

notes: Chapter has a single source page (the primer solution); no separate concept pages were crawled.

definition.text: A graph or tree search that starts at a root and explores all nodes at the current depth before moving to the next depth level.

facts.text: BFS keeps a queue of nodes met but not yet explored, labels each vertex explored when it is enqueued, and stores a parent link on each vertex. The parent links trace the shortest path back to the root.
BFS uses a first-in-first-out queue where depth-first search uses a last-in-first-out stack. On a tree, replacing the queue with a stack turns BFS into depth-first search.

It finds the path with the fewest edges between two nodes, an advantage over depth-first search. It is also complete: it reaches a goal if one exists, even in an infinite graph where depth-first search can get lost.
Time is O(|V|+|E|), since every vertex and edge is explored in the worst case, and space is O(|V|) when the vertex count is known and extra structures mark queued vertices.

For graphs too large to store, reaching nodes at distance d takes O(b^(d+1)) time and memory, where b is the branching factor, the average out-degree. Depth-first algorithms typically need far less extra memory.
BFS is Dijkstra's algorithm on an unweighted graph, where the priority queue degenerates into a FIFO queue. A breadth-first web crawl captures pages with high PageRank early in the crawl.

definition.text: Finding a path between two vertices of a graph so that the sum of the weights of its edges is as small as possible.

facts.text: A road map is modeled as a graph: vertices are intersections or junctions, edges are road segments weighted by length, travel time or cost, and directed edges model one-way streets.

Algorithm choice depends on the graph: Dijkstra's for single-source with non-negative weights, Bellman–Ford if weights may be negative, A* for a single pair using heuristics, Floyd–Warshall for all pairs.
On an unweighted graph, breadth-first search solves the single-source problem in O(E + V).
On undirected graphs with positive weights, Dijkstra's original algorithm takes O(V²). A binary heap gives O((E + V) log V) and a Fibonacci heap gives O(E + V log V).
The all-pairs problem finds shortest paths between every pair of vertices. Floyd–Warshall solves it in O(V³) on directed graphs without negative cycles.
Bellman–Ford can detect a negative cycle in O(|V||E|). Adding constraints, such as keeping a second metric under a threshold, makes the problem NP-complete and harder to solve.
Real road networks are stochastic and time-dependent: travel time varies with traffic, road work, weather and accidents, and there is no accepted definition of an optimal path under uncertainty.

definition.text: A graph that represents social relations between entities; it is a model of a social network.

facts.text: Relations can be mutual or one-way. On Twitter the relation between users is unidirectional, unlike classical social networks such as Facebook, which makes information propagation closer to how information spreads in real life.
In 2012, Twitter's social graph held 537 million accounts connected by 23.95 billion links.

Social graphs are typically stored in graph databases that use graph query languages to query relationships efficiently. Facebook uses TAO, a custom distributed system optimized for fast reads at massive scale.

The graph personalizes the feed: instead of random posts, the app shows content based on a user's previous interactions, and likes, shares and comments reinforce links between users who enjoy the same content.

title: Six degrees of separation

definition.text: The idea that all people are six or fewer social connections apart, so a chain of friend-of-a-friend links joins any two people.

facts.text: The idea generalizes to an average social distance that is logarithmic in population size. With 30 contacts each, six rounds of handshakes would reach a population as large as the United States.
Watts and Strogatz showed the average path length in a random network is ln N / ln K, with N nodes and K acquaintances per node. For N = 300,000,000 and K = 30 that gives 5.7.

Measured distances are close: the average path length among 240 million Microsoft Messenger users was 6 (2007 study), and on Twitter in 2010 the average distance was 4.67, with nearly everyone five steps or less apart.

Bakhshandeh and colleagues' search technique found an average degree of separation of 3.43 between two random Twitter users with an average of only 67 requests; a near-optimal 3.88 took 13.3 requests.

contested_note: Detractors argue that Milgram's small-world experiment did not demonstrate the six-degrees claim, which they call an academic urban myth.

definition.text: A graph search that finds a shortest path from a start vertex to a goal by running one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal, stopping when the two meet.

facts.text: It is often faster: with branching factor b and start-to-goal distance d, each of the two searches costs O(b^(d/2)), and their sum is much less than the O(b^d) of a single search from start to goal.
The backward search must be able to find, for any node, the parent nodes that have an edge into it. Edges need not be traversable both ways, and a reverse arc uses the forward arc's cost.

The two frontiers collide when a node from one has successors in the opposing frontier. Termination needs care: Goldberg and others explained the correct conditions for bidirectional Dijkstra, and bidirectional A* needs a special stopping criterion.

Like A*, it can be guided by a heuristic estimate of the remaining distance to the goal or from the start. Front-to-front variants estimate to every node of the opposing frontier, which is computationally demanding.

Bidirectional Dijkstra often visits far fewer vertices and relaxes far fewer edges than one-directional Dijkstra on single-pair queries, since each search explores roughly half the space. Contraction hierarchies also answer queries with a bidirectional search.

definition.text: A graph representation that stores, for each vertex, an unordered list of its neighbours.

facts.text: Implementations vary: a hash table from each vertex to an array of neighbours, an array indexed by vertex number pointing to linked lists, or vertex and edge objects, which use more memory but can store data per edge.
Its main operation, listing a vertex's neighbours, takes constant time per neighbour, so the total time is proportional to the vertex's degree.

Testing whether an edge exists is slower: time proportional to the smaller degree of the two vertices for unsorted neighbours, or logarithmic in the degree if neighbours form a sorted array searched by binary search.
For a sparse graph an adjacency list is far more space-efficient than an adjacency matrix: space is proportional to the vertices plus edges, against the square of the vertices for a matrix.
A naive array adjacency list of an undirected graph takes about 8|E| bytes on a 32-bit computer, against |V|²/8 bytes for a bit matrix, so it uses more space when density |E|/|V|² exceeds 1/64.

definition.text: A square matrix representing a finite graph, whose elements show whether pairs of vertices are adjacent.

facts.text: For a simple graph of n vertices it is an n-by-n matrix whose element Aij is 1 if an edge runs from vertex i to vertex j, else 0. The diagonal is 0, as simple graphs have no loops.
An undirected graph gives a symmetric matrix, while a directed graph's matrix can be asymmetric. Edge weights can be stored directly in the elements.
Under the common convention, an undirected vertex's degree is the sum of its row or column. For a directed graph, row sums give out-degrees and column sums give in-degrees.
The matrix tests in constant time whether two vertices are adjacent, but listing a vertex's neighbours means scanning a whole row, which takes O(|V|) time.

Each entry needs one bit, so a directed graph fits in |V|²/8 bytes, and the compactness encourages locality of reference. For a large sparse graph, adjacency lists need less storage; sparse matrix representations store only non-zero entries.
Entry (i, j) of the matrix raised to the power n counts the walks of length n from vertex i to vertex j. The smallest n giving a positive entry is the distance between the two vertices.
